synopsis: Volvo is a precedent for a restricted first release: its published low-speed range is 3–15 km/h, and the cited vendor precedents emphasize constrained rear/reverse interactions rather than coverage of more than 100 site configurations [f1598, f1695, f10469, f10897]. Expert judgment recommends reverse-only, low-speed operation with a brief brake pulse and exclusions for stockpiles, trailer loading and slopes, but this is not a published schedule; Volvo’s 2–3-second braking explicitly alerts the operator to intervene [f1597, f10980]. Volvo’s loader remembers the last slope to avoid braking when reversing down a stockpile, illustrating both a task-specific fix and the false-stop problems created by ordinary work practices [f11520, f11872, f10728]. Its separately fitted Radar Detect system creates a commissioning dependency, and a product liability lawyer expects comparison against Volvo and other competitors as part of a state-of-the-art assessment [f10807, f11133]. An SAE paper dated 27 September 2016 provides an on-road simulation precedent using an instrumented Volvo tractor-trailer with Bendix radar and AEB [f10603]. In the 2018 Uber ATG case, Volvo’s factory collision warning and AEB were disabled; a secondary summary from 2019 attributes this partly to shared radar frequencies, raising analogous but unresolved coexistence questions for multi-OEM sites [f1528, f11255, f11256].

relations.note: Both describe slope memory preventing braking during stockpile descent in reverse.
